slides.title: Who Is Actually Making Money From AI?
lines: A Shark Tank-style investigation of demand, capex, cash economics and the price paid.
EVERYONE HAS REVENUE. WHO HAS CASH?
An AI boom can be real while its financing, return profile and market valuation diverge.

slides.title: Strong sales are not the final verdict
lines: “You sold the shovels. Who paid for the gold rush — and did they earn a return?”
Trace each cash obligation to the party ultimately funding it.

slides.title: Follow the economic chain — not just the stock tickers
lines: One party’s sales may be another party’s capital expenditure.

slides.title: Different businesses have different unit economics
lines: High hardware margins can coexist with customer losses.
Must recover infrastructure costs from paid workloads.
May pay for training and inference before monetising.
Must justify software spend with productivity value.
The existence of demand is separate from who captures its economic value.

slides.title: A booking is not a bank deposit
lines: Record actual contract terms, commitments, credits and counterparty concentration.

slides.title: Backlog is neither revenue nor cash
lines: A firm order or committed future spend can improve demand visibility and production planning.
Timing, credits, concentration, cancellations, collection risk and expensive fulfilment dilute economic value.
Check contract enforceability and cash collection — not just a backlog headline.

slides.title: Demand has to become economically useful utilisation
lines: Servers, GPUs, network, energy, land and buildings
What share of capacity is actually used and paid for?
Price per compute task minus energy, support and other costs
Can prices and cash returns outrun chip obsolescence?

slides.title: Four statements, four different questions
lines: Net income, revenue, cash from operations and free cash flow are not synonyms.

slides.title: A cash-flow statement can challenge the revenue headline
lines: Completely hypothetical company; amounts in USD billions.
Operating cash flow +$60bn  |  Cash PP&E –$75bn  |  Simple FCF –$15bn
Simple issuer-style FCF = CFO − cash PP&E purchases. Definitions differ by issuer.

slides.title: The first cash-flow test
lines: An example of a heavy build-out, not evidence a real company is failing.
Negative FCF alone is neither a fraud test nor a final business verdict.

slides.title: What the simple calculation might miss
lines: Equipment purchased with cash is normally an investing cash-flow outflow, subject to statement presentation.
Equipment additions and principal payments can follow different balance-sheet/cash-flow treatment. Read the notes.
Compare issuers after normalising definitions, funding vehicles and timing.

slides.title: Useful life is an assumption with real consequences
lines: Capitalised asset cost is typically expensed over a useful life. Estimate changes can affect period earnings.
Equipment may still need replacing sooner due to performance-per-watt improvements or product demand.
Depreciation policy does not prove physical chip life or investment payback.

slides.title: Quarterly FCF is not trailing-twelve-month FCF
lines: Illustrative four-quarter sequence; label the exact reporting dates in real comparisons.
A single quarterly number can be influenced by delivery and payment timing.

slides.title: A supplier can win before the customer proves its ROI
lines: Records product revenue if delivery/recognition criteria are met.
Pays cash or commits financing to capacity.
Needs paid task demand and adequate net margins.
A hardware cycle can be profitable even if parts of downstream investment disappoint.

slides.title: What does the new investment actually earn?
lines: INCREMENTAL ROIC ≈ Δ NOPAT / Δ CAPITAL
Return > funding cost? Not just revenue > last year.
Need attribution, tax basis, ramp-up lag and asset-life assumptions.
ROIC and WACC should be compared on a compatible capital/return basis.

slides.title: Great technology can still be a poor investment
lines: Paid demand, pricing power, sustainable returns, financing resilience and cash conversion.
What future performance is already assumed by the valuation? What breaks the expectation?
Business success and share-price upside are different claims.

slides.title: The financing questions the Sharks would ask
lines: What comes due before the capacity pays for itself?
Cash, committed facilities and covenant headroom
Minimum repayments and future infrastructure needs
What happens if one strategic counterparty slows?

slides.title: Some AI spending can circulate within the same ecosystem
lines: Circularity is a diligence question. Do not call a deal fraudulent without evidence.

slides.title: The same capex boom can end three ways
lines: New workloads monetise; utilisation and FCF improve.
Demand grows, but margins and returns compress.
Capacity overshoots; financing tightens; replacement spend persists.
Scenarios are conditional branches, not asserted probabilities.

slides.title: What evidence would actually settle the debate?
lines: CFO, cash capex, lease principal on comparable bases
Delivered workloads, cash collections, gross margin quality
Incremental return above relevant cost of capital
Debt maturity, covenants, financing costs and customer concentration

slides.title: The bull and bear each need better evidence
lines: Enterprise AI creates durable paid savings; higher future margins justify front-loaded investment.
Spend reflects competitive pressure and interdependent financing; future free cash flow fails to catch up.
Do not mistake a conclusion about profitability for a recommendation on entry price.

slides.title: A five-question investor card
lines: Identify the end payer and what is already collected.
Track durable gross margin, operating profit and cash.
Map leases, debt, equity issuance and capex schedule.
Compare scenario cash returns with valuation expectations.
Name the demand, obsolescence and financing falsifiers.
The Shark Tank lens is a questioning framework, not a recommendation.

slides.title: The three tests that stop bad AI earnings takes
lines: Does a $5bn order automatically mean $5bn cash paid?
Can a chip supplier earn more while a buyer earns poor ROI?
Bonus: Does negative FCF alone prove wrongdoing? No.
